text: Every CLI command that queries the SQLite cache (e.g. `tick ready`) fails deterministically with `Error: failed to query tasks: SQL logic error: no such column: t.type (1)` when the project's `.tick/cache.db` predates schema changes that added new columns such as `type`; reproducible always under that condition, on all platforms.

cites.section: Bug: Missing Schema Evolution in SQLite Cache

text: `ensureFresh()` lazily opens the cache via `OpenCache()`, which runs `schemaSQL` with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`; that is a no-op on an existing table and adds no missing columns, so an old `tasks` table without `type` passes. `IsFresh()` then succeeds because the `metadata` table exists in old schemas. If the JSONL hash matches, no rebuild runs and the caller's query fails on `t.type`; if the hash differs, `Rebuild()`'s INSERT naming the `type` column fails and surfaces as "failed to rebuild cache".
how: Code trace of internal/storage/store.go ensureFresh and internal/storage/cache.go OpenCache, IsFresh and Rebuild.

text: Root cause: the cache has a content-freshness model (SHA256 hash of the JSONL) but no schema-freshness model; nothing detects when the schema defined in code has diverged from the on-disk cache schema, and `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` silently accepts the old one.
how: Analysis of the code trace, restated in the approved spec.

cites.section: Bug: Missing Schema Evolution in SQLite Cache

text: The existing corruption recovery in `ensureFresh()` catches only `IsFresh()` query errors, which never occur here because the `metadata` table exists in old schemas, so the error surfaces later in queries or rebuilds; and no schema version was tracked in the metadata table.
how: Read from the code trace of store.go's corruption recovery.

text: Tests never caught it because every test starts from a fresh `t.TempDir()` and so never meets a pre-existing cache with an old schema; the bug shows only on upgrade, a scenario no unit test covered.
how: Read from the test setup pattern.

text: Blast radius: every CLI command that queries the cache, and the upgrade path for all existing users; any future schema change would cause the same failure unless versioning is added.
how: Read from the analysis.

text: How should the cache detect and recover from a schema that has changed since the cache.db was created?
Add a hard-coded integer schema version constant, `const schemaVersion = 1`, in `cache.go`.
why: The cache is ephemeral and rebuilt from JSONL, so an explicit version number marking each schema change is enough to detect a stale schema.

text: `Rebuild()` stores `schema_version` in the existing `metadata` table alongside `jsonl_hash`.
why: The metadata table already holds the JSONL hash and is the right place for the version.

text: Early in `ensureFresh()`, before `IsFresh()`, query `metadata` for key `schema_version` and compare it with `schemaVersion`.
why: Checking before `IsFresh()` avoids querying a schema-incompatible cache.

text: If the stored version is missing or differs from `schemaVersion`, close the DB, delete the cache file, reopen it and force a rebuild from JSONL.
why: The cache is ephemeral by design, so a full delete and rebuild is the correct recovery.

text: On a new cache the missing version triggers the same delete+rebuild path; the extra cycle is accepted.
why: Cache creation is infrequent.

text: Increment `schemaVersion` whenever `schemaSQL` changes in future; that is all a future schema change requires.
why: The version only detects a stale schema if every schema change bumps it.

text: Use a simple integer version, not a hash of the `schemaSQL` string.
why: An integer is explicit and conventional; hashing the SQL would trigger needless rebuilds on whitespace or comment changes and is harder to reason about.
rules_out: Hashing the schemaSQL string and comparing the hash

text: No `ALTER TABLE` migrations for the cache.
why: The cache is ephemeral by design and rebuilds in milliseconds; a migration framework would be over-engineered for it.
rules_out: ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN migrations preserving existing cache data

text: Do not delete and rebuild the cache on every startup.
why: It would destroy the performance benefit of caching and defeat hash-based freshness; most startups need no rebuild.
rules_out: Always deleting and rebuilding the cache on startup

text: The change is confined to `internal/storage/cache.go` (version constant, storing the version on rebuild, a version check function) and `internal/storage/store.go` (the early check in `ensureFresh()` triggering delete+rebuild on mismatch).
why: The fix touches only the cache lifecycle.

Test that a cache with a wrong schema version triggers delete + rebuild.
why: Covers the version-mismatch path.

text: Test that a cache with a missing schema version (a pre-versioning cache.db) triggers delete + rebuild.
why: Covers the upgrade case that caused the bug.

text: Test that a cache with a matching schema version is preserved, with no unnecessary rebuild.
why: Guards the caching benefit.

text: Test that after a version-triggered rebuild, queries succeed normally.
why: Confirms the fix removes the reported query failure.

text: When a status transition triggers cascades, the output includes '(unchanged)' lines for sibling and descendant tasks that were already in a terminal state before the command ran (e.g. `tick done tick-b15fda` prints three '<id>: done (unchanged)' lines after the primary and auto-cascaded transitions); in deeper hierarchies these lines can outnumber the real transitions.
how: Reported and reproduced from the CLI output of a cascading `tick done`.

text: The noise reproduces always: create a parent with several children, complete some children individually, then complete the last non-terminal child; the output lists '(unchanged)' entries for the already-completed siblings.

text: Impact is low severity and output clarity only: it affects all users performing cascade transitions, with no data correctness issue.
how: Impact assessment in the investigation.

text: `RunTransition()` in internal/cli/transition.go (start/done/cancel/reopen) calls `sm.ApplyUserTransition()` and, when cascades exist, `buildCascadeResult()`, which builds `Cascaded` entries from the real cascade changes, builds an `involvedIDs` set (primary plus cascaded tasks), then walks all tasks to add terminal children of involved tasks not in that set to `cr.Unchanged`; `outputTransitionOrCascade()` in helpers.go routes the result to `FormatCascadeTransition()`.
how: Traced through the code.

text: All three formatters render the unchanged entries: toon as '{id}: {status} (unchanged)', pretty as a tree node labelled '(unchanged)', and JSON as an `unchanged` array.
how: Traced through the formatter code.

text: Root cause: the unchanged collection is intentional code, not a logic bug. Lines 117-135 of `buildCascadeResult()` deliberately walk descendants of involved tasks and collect terminal ones not part of the cascade into `CascadeResult.Unchanged`; the design was built to show what did not change alongside what did, and the resulting noise outweighs any transparency benefit, since an unchanged task carries no actionable information.
how: Read from the code during the investigation.

text: Contributing factors: the `Unchanged` field and `UnchangedEntry` type are part of the `CascadeResult` struct, so every formatter must handle them, and tests actively validate unchanged collection and rendering, reinforcing the behaviour as correct.
how: Read from the code and tests.

text: This is not a regression but original behaviour: small hierarchies (one or two unchanged lines) are tolerable, and the problem shows with deeper trees where unchanged entries outnumber real transitions.
how: Assessment in the investigation.

text: Blast radius: directly affected are internal/cli/transition.go, format.go, toon_formatter.go, pretty_formatter.go, json_formatter.go and the tests asserting unchanged behaviour; potentially affected are external consumers parsing JSON output that depend on the `unchanged` array (unlikely but possible).
how: Read from the code during the investigation.

text: How should the cascade unchanged noise be fixed?
Remove the unchanged feature entirely: a clean deletion with no new behaviour, no flags and no conditional logic.

Keeping the JSON unchanged array for backwards compatibility

text: After the fix, cascade output lists only the primary transition and the genuinely cascaded changes: `tick done tick-b15fda` prints the primary 'in_progress → done' line and the '(auto)' cascade lines, and no '(unchanged)' lines.

text: In `buildCascadeResult()` in internal/cli/transition.go, remove the unchanged collection loop (lines 117-135) and the `involvedIDs` map (lines 110-115), which exists solely to support the loop and becomes dead code without it.

text: Remove the `UnchangedEntry` type and the `Unchanged` field from `CascadeResult` in internal/cli/format.go.

text: Remove unchanged rendering from all three formatters: the toon formatter's unchanged lines, the pretty formatter's unchanged tree rendering, and the JSON formatter's unchanged array.

text: The fix introduces no new behaviour; state and cascade logic stay untouched, and only output construction and rendering change.

text: Running `tick note tree --foo` produces the error `unknown flag "--foo" for "note tree"`, which misleadingly implies "note tree" is a real command that only rejects that flag. Reproducible always.
how: Reproduced by running the command, as the investigation's reproduction steps record.

text: Running `tick note tree` without flags produces `unknown note sub-command 'tree'`: correct, but reached by a path inconsistent with the flagged case, since flag validation passes with no flag arguments and `handleNote` (note.go:33) rejects the subcommand.
how: Reproduced by running the command, as the investigation's reproduction steps record; the path traced by reading the code.

text: Impact is low severity on an unlikely user path: poor UX for an edge case through a misleading error message.
how: Assessed in the investigation's symptoms.

text: The bug surfaced during the dep-tree-visualization review, in the `qualifyCommand` switch in `internal/cli/app.go`.
how: Recorded in the investigation's references.

text: `qualifyCommand(subcmd, subArgs)` (app.go:100) runs before flag validation; for `note` with `["tree", "--foo"]` it passes the parent gate (app.go:367), matches the shared `"add", "remove", "tree"` case and returns `("note tree", ["--foo"])`; `ValidateFlags("note tree", ...)` (flags.go:116-147) then looks up a key absent from `commandFlags`, gets a nil map, and the failed flag lookup yields the misleading error.
how: Traced by reading internal/cli/app.go, flags.go and note.go.

text: Root cause: the `qualifyCommand` switch (app.go:374-376) groups `"add"`, `"remove"`, `"tree"` in one case for both `dep` and `note` parents with no parent-specific guard, so `"tree"`, valid only under `dep`, is qualified under `note` too. `"add"` and `"remove"` are legitimately shared.
how: Read from the code; the investigation's synthesis validation confirmed it with high confidence and found no gaps.

text: Contributing factors: `qualifyCommand` checks the parent's identity but then uses one undifferentiated switch for all subcommands; the grouped pattern worked until the dep-only `"tree"` was added; and `commandFlags` validates flags only, not command existence, so the qualified name is trusted.
how: Read from the code.

text: It was not caught because no test covers `qualifyCommand("note", ["tree", ...])` (existing tests cover only the `dep` parent); the flag-validation test lists rightly omit `"note tree"`; the drift-detection test checks `commandFlags` against the help registry, not against `qualifyCommand`'s output space; and the user gets an error either way, so manual testing is unlikely to notice.
how: Read from the tests and code.

text: Blast radius: only `tick note tree` with flags is affected (misleading error); without flags it works correctly. No other subcommand leaks, as `"add"` and `"remove"` are legitimately shared between `dep` and `note`.
how: Read from the code.

why: Minimal change, clear intent, no behavioural change for any valid command path; `"tree"` is the only dep-specific subcommand, so the current structure is simple enough.
rules_out: Fully splitting into parent-specific switch blocks for `dep` and `note`: more verbose, though it would prevent future leaks of new parent-specific subcommands.
alternatives: Split "tree" into a dep-guarded case (chosen).
Fully split into parent-specific switches.

text: The shared `"add", "remove"` case remains for both `dep` and `note` parents.
why: `"add"` and `"remove"` are legitimately valid under both parents.

text: When `subcmd == "note"` and the subcommand is `"tree"`, `qualifyCommand` does not qualify it: it returns the original command and args unchanged, letting `handleNote` produce the correct error.

text: Unknown flags passed to any tick command are silently discarded: any argument starting with '-' that is not a known flag is stripped without warning or error, and the command runs as if it were absent, which can mislead users into thinking the flag had effect. Example: 'tick dep add tick-aaa --blocks tick-bbb' succeeds, ignoring --blocks (valid only on create/update) and behaving as 'tick dep add tick-aaa tick-bbb'. Reproducible always.

text: Layer 1, global parsing: parseArgs() in app.go (lines 317-339) extracts known global flags (--quiet, --verbose, --toon, --pretty, --json, --help) via applyGlobalFlag() and silently skips any unknown flag appearing before the subcommand; after the subcommand is found, all remaining args, unknown flags included, are passed to the command handler as rest.

text: Layer 2, per-command parsing: every command hand-rolls its own flag parsing with the same silent skip of unknown flags: dep.go (40-43) and note.go (43-44) skip every '-' argument when extracting positionals; create.go (93-94) and update.go (111-112) fall through a 'strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-")' switch case commented 'global flags already extracted'; remove.go (29-30) has the same case commented 'Skip unknown flags.'; list.go (34-102) switches on known flags and lets unknown ones fall through; show.go and transition.go take args[0] as the task ID and ignore any flags.

The 'global flags already extracted' comments are misleading, since global parsing is also non-validating.

text: How should the CLI reject unknown flags: where does validation live, and where does each command's flag knowledge live?

text: The flow: parseArgs() strips global flags, identifies the subcommand and collects rest; the valid flags for the identified command are looked up and rest is validated against them, erroring on any unknown flag; then the command handler is dispatched, and can assume all flags are valid.

text: How should hierarchy work: as an organizational grouping or as a workflow constraint?
When an unblocked task has children, should `tick ready` return the parent, only its leaf children, or both?
Parent/child is organizational: a parent groups related tasks and does not block them, children being decomposition and context for the parent; `blocked_by` is what controls workflow.
why: Two distinct relationships: hierarchy says a task is part of a larger thing, dependencies say it cannot start until others are done.

text: There is one task entity: subtasks use the same schema as tasks, hierarchy expressed by the `parent` field alone, with no `type` field and no special epic or subtask handling.
why: With `type` removed, a task with children is in effect an epic.

text: Only leaf work appears in `tick ready`: a task with open children (status `open` or `in_progress`) is not ready, its children being the work; once all its children are closed it becomes a leaf and can appear. This replaces the log's "parent readiness determined only by explicit blocked_by" and its leaving ready behaviour to implementation.
why: The ready list is then the actual work items, with no extra lookups; returning the parent makes the agent look up its children, and returning both clutters the list and invites starting the parent before its children.
rules_out: Returning the unblocked parent and leaving the agent to find its children
Returning parent and children together

text: An unclosed dependency blocker on any ancestor, walked up the full parent chain to the root, makes its open descendants not ready; an ancestor's open children do not propagate this way.
why: Children of a dependency-blocked parent otherwise appear ready though their parent cannot be worked; an intermediate grouping task with no blockers of its own would hide the block from an immediate-parent check; propagating open children would leave no leaf ever ready.
rules_out: Checking the immediate parent only
Propagating the open-children state to descendants

text: With JSONL as source of truth and SQLite as query cache, how are the two kept in sync, and what happens when they diverge?

cites.section: Discussion: Freshness Check & Dual Write Implementation > Context

text: SQLite is a cache, not a peer: tasks.jsonl is the git-committed source of truth, SQLite is an expendable local cache that can always be rebuilt from JSONL, and mismatches self-heal on the next read. No sync commands.
why: Treating SQLite as rebuildable turns the problem from preventing inconsistency into detecting and recovering from it, which the freshness check already does; this removes the need for two-phase commits or complex sync logic.

text: The cache lives at .tick/cache.db (gitignored) beside .tick/tasks.jsonl (git tracked), with a separate .tick/lock file for concurrent access.
why: The approved spec fixes the layout; it replaces the .cache/tick.db path the log's context and the research used.

text: Hash or mtime for freshness detection: what are the trade-offs, and the cross-platform considerations?

cites.section: Hash vs mtime for freshness detection? > Context

text: Freshness is detected by a SHA256 hash of the tasks.jsonl contents, compared with the hash stored in the SQLite metadata table under key jsonl_hash; SHA256 comes from Go's stdlib crypto/sha256.
why: A content hash is definitive: if content changed, the hash changed. mtime misses changes for an agent-first tool: git operations can disturb mtime, fast agents may edit within the same second, and cross-platform consistency matters.
rules_out: mtime comparison: misses same-second edits, clock skew, git operations that preserve mtime
Hybrid mtime + size with hash on mismatch: more complex and still vulnerable to mtime issues

Option C: Hybrid (mtime + size, hash on mismatch)

text: On every operation tick reads tasks.jsonl fully into memory and computes its hash; on a mismatch it rebuilds SQLite from the data already in memory, with no second read.
why: The file is read anyway on a cache miss, so hashing data already in memory is negligible. Trade-off accepted: always reading the full file is acceptable for expected file sizes (<1MB, <10ms).

text: How are partial write failures handled: what if the JSONL write succeeds but SQLite fails, or the reverse?

cites.section: How to handle partial write failures? > Context

text: Mutations are JSONL-first: the new JSONL is written (atomic temp + rename) before SQLite is updated; if the SQLite update fails, tick logs a warning and continues, and the next read detects the hash mismatch and rebuilds SQLite.
why: SQLite can always be rebuilt from JSONL, so inconsistency only needs detecting and recovering, which the freshness check does. Trade-off accepted: an SQLite failure costs one rebuild on the next read, acceptable given the simplicity gained.
rules_out: True two-phase commit across SQLite and JSONL: complex, overkill
SQLite-first with JSONL regenerated from SQLite: inverts the source-of-truth model
alternatives: Option B: True two-phase commit
Option C: SQLite-first with JSONL regeneration

How to handle partial write failures? > Decision

text: The stored hash is updated on every mutation, in the same SQLite transaction as the data change (BEGIN; apply mutation; UPDATE metadata SET jsonl_hash = new hash; COMMIT).
why: Without updating the stored hash after a successful JSONL write, every later read would see a mismatch and rebuild. If the transaction fails, both the data and the hash update are lost together, which is correct: the next read sees JSONL's new content against the old hash and rebuilds, applying the lost change.

text: The eriner/jsonl Go package documents JSONL as inherently power-loss resistant: each line is atomic, so an interrupted write corrupts only that line and earlier lines stay intact; the package is designed for write-error recoverable applications.

Is full file rewrite acceptable for updates? > References

text: Taskwarrior's corruption issues stem from concurrent access without file locking, shell prompt integrations running parallel commands among them; the lesson drawn is that file locking is essential.
how: Researched Taskwarrior's issue tracker (https://github.com/GothenburgBitFactory/taskwarrior/issues/2070).

Is full file rewrite acceptable for updates? > References

text: Every mutation (create, update, delete) rewrites the whole tasks.jsonl atomically; there is no append-only mode, one code path for all mutations.
why: Atomic rename guarantees a complete file or no change, while append can leave an incomplete last line; one strategy gives a simpler mental model. Performance: ~500 tasks x ~200 bytes = 100KB, so write + fsync + rename is trivially fast.

Append-only log with compaction: tombstones, versioning and compaction are a complexity explosion
SQLite as source of truth: binary file in git, inverts the model, still needs JSONL export

How do we ensure data integrity on writes? > Journey
How do we ensure data integrity on writes? > Decision

text: Write operations take an exclusive lock on .tick/lock, blocking other readers and writers.
why: Prevents concurrent access corruption.

cites.section: How do we ensure data integrity on writes? > Decision

text: Read operations take a shared lock on .tick/lock: other readers are allowed and writers blocked, so concurrent reads are safe, and a pending write waits for all readers to finish.
why: Allows concurrent reads while keeping writes safe.

cites.section: How do we ensure data integrity on writes? > Decision

text: Lock acquisition times out after 5 seconds by default; on timeout tick returns the error "Error: Could not acquire lock on .tick/lock - another process may be using tick" and does not proceed. A lock held for long (e.g. a crashed process) can be cleared by deleting .tick/lock by hand.
why: The approved spec sets the timeout and its handling.

text: Every mutation (create, update, delete) runs: acquire exclusive lock on .tick/lock; read tasks.jsonl, compute hash, check freshness (rebuild if stale); apply mutation in memory; write complete new content to a temp file; fsync it; os.Rename(temp, tasks.jsonl); update SQLite in one transaction applying the mutation and storing the new hash; release the lock.
why: Combines the locking, freshness, atomic rewrite and JSONL-first decisions into one sequence.

text: What should the default output format be for each command type?

cites.section: Q1: Default Output Format > Options Considered

text: The output format is auto-detected from stdout: piped or redirected (no TTY) gives TOON, the default for agents; a terminal (TTY) gives human-readable output. tick doctor is the exception: it outputs human-readable text only, with no TOON or JSON variant.
why: Agents run commands through a pipe, so they get TOON without remembering a flag, and humans at a terminal get readable output; it is the established Unix pattern of ls, git and grep. The doctor spec, a later answer, sets doctor apart: it is a debugging tool run by humans, agents do not parse diagnostics, and structured output would be complexity for no real use case.
rules_out: Always TOON, requiring --pretty for human-readable output (humans see cryptic output by default)
Human-readable by default, requiring --toon for agents (agents must always remember the flag)

cites.section: Why This Works Perfectly for Agents

text: Every command but tick doctor takes the override flags --toon (force TOON), --pretty (force human-readable) and --json (force JSON); doctor has no TOON or JSON variant to force.
why: Explicit flags cover the edge cases auto-detection does not, such as a human in a script wanting readable output. The doctor spec, a later answer, gives doctor human-readable text only.
rules_out: The research's --plain flag for human-readable output: --pretty takes its place

text: TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) is a format designed for LLM consumption that achieves 30-60% token savings over JSON while improving parsing accuracy (73.9% vs 69.7% in benchmarks). Agents consume tick output frequently (every `tick ready` call), so token efficiency bears directly on cost and context window usage.

Storage stays JSONL; TOON is the default output format, for agent consumption.
why: Token efficiency is critical for output and irrelevant for storage; JSONL keeps clean line-by-line git diffs and universal parser maturity, while TOON suits uniform arrays such as `tick ready` and `tick list`.

cites.section: What validations should doctor perform? > Decision

text: Error check: JSONL syntax errors, meaning any line tick cannot load as a task — malformed JSON, or valid JSON of the wrong shape or type — fails the JSONL check with its line named.
why: Checking only that a line parses as JSON let doctor report healthy a store no command could open: a valid-JSON line tick cannot load (`"priority":"high"`, `null`, `{}`, a whitespace-only line) makes every command fail while a JSON-only check passes it, and the cache advice then points at a `rebuild` that fails the same way. text: Passing `--quiet` and a field selection together is refused: an error with a non-zero exit and nothing on stdout.
why: `--quiet` prints a bare task ID and a single-field request prints a bare value; two different single values have been asked for, and silently picking one hands back something the caller did not ask for.

text: How can free text that begins with a dash — a note or a title — be written back, when the flag check rejects it?

A note beginning with a dash is refused with `unknown flag "- read the header" for "note add"`, and `tick create "- some title"` is refused identically: `ValidateFlags` inspects every argument beginning with `-` that is not numeric and not a global flag and rejects any not in the command's flag set (`grep -n 'func ValidateFlags' -A 30 internal/cli/flags.go` → flags.go:117-147). `--description` escapes only because its value follows a registered value-taking flag.
how: Measured by running the commands; the code was located by grep.

text: The unknown-flag check itself is kept; the fix is confined to its being applied to arguments that are free text by definition.
why: It exists so `tick update tick-a1b2 --prioirty 3` refuses rather than silently reporting success.

text: The free-text argument problem is fixed as part of this work, not left as a follow-up.
why: It is the one place the round-trip guarantee has a hole — text an agent can read out of tick and cannot put back — and leaving it ships the contract with an exception nobody wrote down.

text: `--` was rejected only as a bare argument (`unknown flag "--" for "note add"`); as the value of a registered value-taking flag it was accepted and stored — `tick update <id> --description --` stored the two-dash description, because `ValidateFlags` skipped the argument after a `TakesValue` flag and `applyGlobalFlag` never claimed `--` — and it fails with `--description requires a value` once the marker is recognised at any position.
how: Verified by building the commit preceding the phase (`b9782df7`), as the specification's corrigendum records; no command is given.

text: `--` is supported as the end-of-flags marker and becomes the canonical documented way to pass free text that may begin with a dash. Nothing after it is read as a flag — neither the command's own flags nor the global format flags — so free text spelling a flag exactly, such as a note reading `--json`, is writable too.
why: It is almost entirely additive: `--` was rejected as a bare argument on every command, so inputs that failed begin to succeed. One case changes — `--` as the value of a value-taking flag — which the marker alone cannot restore.

text: The attached form `--flag=value` is the repair for a value the marker now claims, and it closes with it the pre-existing sibling case where a value spelling a global flag is stripped wherever it appears.
why: A post-marker argument is a positional and can never re-attach to the flag, so the marker alone cannot restore `--description --`.

text: Flag inspection stops after the task ID on `note add`, so a dash-leading note that is not itself a global flag works with or without the marker. What stops is the check, not flag handling: global flags are still consumed wherever they appear (`sed -n '352,373p' internal/cli/app.go`), so `tick note add <id> "text" --json` prints JSON as before and note text spelling a global flag exactly still needs the marker.
why: `note add` registers no flags (`grep -n '"note add":' internal/cli/flags.go` → flags.go:80, `"note add": {}`), so nothing after the ID could be a flag the check would catch, and refusing it is the whole defect.

text: The existing bare-argument form keeps working: `--` is the recommended form, not a required one.
why: Nothing that works as a bare argument today stops working.

text: `create` does not stop flag inspection and relies on `--` for a dash-leading title.
why: Its title shares the argument list with real flags (`--priority`, `--description`), so a dash-leading title is indistinguishable from a mistyped flag without a marker.

text: Do very large descriptions strain the argument list enough to need a stdin or file input path?
The argument limit is 1 MiB, and passing a 200 KB argument through a process call succeeds; a real task description from a live project runs to roughly 4.5 KB, under half a percent of the limit.
how: Measured on this system.

text: The store's reader stopped at any task line of 65,536 bytes, so a description past that was accepted, written, and then made every command, `rebuild` included, fail until `tasks.jsonl` was edited by hand; `oversized-text-field-bricks-the-store` removes the reader's ceiling and caps the description.
how: Recorded by the specification's corrigendum from that work unit.

text: Descriptions are passed as command-line arguments; no stdin or file input path is added. Descriptions are capped at a finite character limit, its value set by `oversized-text-field-bricks-the-store`, as note text is capped at 2000 characters (`grep -n 'maxNoteTextLen' internal/task/notes.go` → notes.go:12).
why: The caps sit far inside the argument limit, so an input path for a larger description would serve a case that cannot occur.

text: What verification keeps the output conformant after this work, so the next change cannot add a hand-built section and break it again?

The existing suite compares output against strings written alongside the code, so a malformed header passed for the tool's entire life — the test compared a wrong string to the same wrong string — and every one of those assertions has to be rewritten regardless, since every shape this work touches changes.
how: Read from the test suite.

text: Every structured command's output is decoded by a real TOON reader in the suite, and the test fails if it will not parse. Coverage is counted in documents rather than commands: every branch a must-parse command can take, the emptied dep-tree forms included, and every document `show` produces, a multi-field selection and one narrowed by position included.
why: This alone catches the entire class of defect this work fixes — a section nobody can read, whatever its content.

text: One deliberately awkward task is a permanent fixture, round-tripped end to end: free text with newlines, quotes, commas, a leading dash, trailing spaces at the end of an interior line, and a line that looks like a section header, carried in all three free-text carriers — the title and the note text beginning with a dash, the description carrying the multi-line content. Write it in, read it out, decode it, write the decoded text back (a note by adding it again, asserting on the new note), and assert the stored value is byte-for-byte what it was.
why: It is the only test that checks the guarantee this work made, the round trip, rather than parseability; it would have caught the description, tags item-marker and refs comma defects. Edge whitespace is trimmed on the way in, so the trailing spaces sit mid-text.

text: Rewritten assertions check decoded values, not output text: "the notes section has two rows and the second row's text is X", not "the output equals this blob".
why: Decoded-value assertions survive harmless reformatting while still failing when a section goes missing or a value is wrong.

text: No byte-level pinning is kept in the machine formats, toon and JSON.
why: Golden strings pin the exact output shape, but they are the mechanism that rotted into the defect this work undoes; the user took that trade for toon and JSON.

text: Pretty keeps golden-string assertions.
why: Pretty output has no parser, so a decoded-value assertion does not exist for it; removing its golden strings would replace its only form of assertion with nothing.
